explanation:
Starting with A gets you to B. The second premise starts at C and gets you to D. Add B → C and the chain becomes A → B → C → D.

Why the others fail: A joins C to B in the wrong direction. B reverses the second premise. D takes you back to A. E reverses the target rather than establishing it.

Contrapose C̸ → B̸ to obtain B → C. Now A leads to B and then C. C → D finishes the chain.

Why the others fail: A runs from the destination back toward C. B loops back to A. C requires C̸, but the premises give C when A occurs. E begins at D, which is what you still need to reach.

A gives B̸, not B. The bridge must let you move from B̸ to C. Then C gives D.

Why the others fail: A requires B. B and C merely make B̸ a result; neither lets you start from B̸ and reach C. D reverses the second premise.

Adding A → B creates D → A → B → L. Contrapose the chain: L̸ → B̸ → A̸ → D̸. That is the conclusion.

Why the others fail: B points across the gap backward. C starts from A̸, although D supplies A. D reverses D → L. E sends A to B̸, which does not establish L or exclude D when L is absent.

A already gives B. The second rule needs B and C together. Adding A → C supplies C whenever A occurs, so the full trigger is satisfied and D follows.

Why the others fail: A does not give C from A. C and D begin with the result you need to prove. E says what happens without A; it says nothing that supplies C when A occurs.

A guarantees at least one of B and C. The B branch already reaches D. C → D makes the other branch reach D too. Either way, A guarantees D.

Why the others fail: A and E begin with D. B sends C back to A without ensuring D. D rules out B when A occurs, forcing C, but still gives no path from C to D.

premises: If a visitor's badge is scanned, that visitor is admitted.
A visitor is admitted only if that visitor's registration is current.

choices.text: Every visitor whose badge is scanned is an invited guest.
Every visitor with current registration is an invited guest.
No invited guest has their badge scanned.
Every invited guest has their badge scanned.
Every admitted visitor is an invited guest.

explanation:
Let G = invited guest, B = badge scanned, E = admitted, R = registration current. The premises give B → E → R. Add G → B to obtain G → B → E → R.

Why the others fail: A, B and E make guest status a result, not a starting point that guarantees registration. C blocks the badge condition without ruling out guest status or establishing registration.
conclusion: Every invited guest has current registration

premises: Entering the facility requires a valid pass.
For this exercise, evaluate the person's sole pass. C = canceled; X = expired; V = valid; E = permitted to enter using that pass.

choices.text: Every pass that is not canceled is expired.

explanation:
No expired pass is valid means X → V̸. Entry requires validity: E → V, so V̸ → E̸. Add C → X and canceled leads to expired, invalid, and therefore no entry using that pass.

Why the others fail: B reverses the needed connection. C addresses passes that are not canceled. D establishes validity rather than excluding entry. E gives another route into the facility, not a reason canceled passes cannot be used.
conclusion: Anyone holding only a canceled pass cannot enter the facility

premises: A shipment cannot leave unless it has been inspected.
Inspection guarantees that the shipment is sealed.
explanation:
Let L = can leave, I = inspected, S = sealed, F = flagged. The premises give L → I → S. Therefore S̸ → I̸ → L̸. Adding F → S̸ establishes F → L̸.

Why the others fail: A reverses the bridge. C supplies a necessary condition for departure without ruling departure out. D makes flagged status a result, not a trigger for being uninspected. E supplies permission to leave rather than preventing it.

premises: Every finalist submits a sample or completes an interview.
No applicant who completes an interview lacks approval.
Applicants receive approval unless a review is pending.

choices.text: Every applicant without a pending review submits a sample.
Every applicant with a pending review submits a sample.
Every applicant who submits a sample has a pending review.
Every approved applicant submits a sample.
No applicant who submits a sample has a pending review.

explanation:
Let F = finalist, S = sample, J = interview, A = approval, P = pending review. The rules are F → S or J, J → A, and P̸ → A. The interview branch already reaches approval. E supplies S → P̸, so the sample branch also reaches approval. Both alternatives now support F → A.

Why the others fail: A points from no pending review to sample, not from sample to no pending review. B and C connect samples with a pending review, which does not establish approval. D reverses a possible connection from samples to approval.
A gives B, and B gives C. So A → C. A, D and E reverse valid arrows. B incorrectly treats the absence of A as ruling out C.
The second premise contraposes to B → C. Join it to A → B. A and B reverse what is established. C negates the result. E infers from the absence of the starting condition.

choices.text: At least one of A and B is true.

explanation: C̸ gives B̸, and B̸ gives A̸. Here a fact activates the contrapositive chain. Every other option conflicts with the resulting facts.

A is already established. If B also occurs, both parts of the trigger hold, producing C and then D. B incorrectly treats A alone as enough. C and E reverse arrows. D rules out D merely because this particular trigger is incomplete.

choices.text: Both B and C are true.

explanation: A guarantees at least one of B and C. C is ruled out, so B must hold. A rejects the remaining alternative. C and D conflict with C̸. E contradicts the stated fact A.

Either available branch reaches D. You do not need to know which branch occurs. A reverses the resulting rule. B and D select one alternative without support. E rules out D when A is absent, even though D could occur another way.

choices.text: Every certified staff member is an editor.
No person who is not an editor is certified.
Everyone who reviews submissions is an editor.
Every certified staff member reviews submissions.

explanation: Editor → reviewer. “Only certified staff” makes certification necessary for reviewing: reviewer → certified. Therefore editor → certified. A, C and E reverse established connections. B infers not certified from not editor.

Damaged → not accepted. Contrapose: accepted → not damaged. Insured → accepted → not damaged. B and D reverse valid relationships. C treats not insured as enough to establish damage. E connects damage to insurance without support.

premises: The machine operates unless the safety switch is off.
The machine operates only if cooling is active.

choices.text: If the safety switch is off, the machine does not operate.
If cooling is not active, the safety switch is off.
If cooling is active, the machine operates.
If the machine does not operate, the safety switch is not off.
If cooling is not active, the safety switch is not off.

explanation: Let S = switch off, O = operates, C = cooling active. The premises give S̸ → O → C. Contrapose the chain: C̸ → O̸ → S. A adds an unwarranted converse to the unless rule. C reverses the cooling requirement. D and E negate the switch condition incorrectly.

premises: Approval is withheld unless the review is complete.
No incomplete application receives a completed review.
A completed review guarantees either a standard award or an exception.
This application receives a research grant but does not receive a standard award.

choices.text: It receives an exception, and it is incomplete.
It receives no exception, and it is complete.
It receives a standard award, and it is complete.
Its review is not complete, and it receives an exception.
It receives an exception, and it is complete.

explanation:
Let G = grant, A = approval, R = completed review, K = complete application, S = standard award, E = exception. Diagram G → A → R. The no rule is K̸ → R̸, so R → K. The guarantee is R → S or E. The grant establishes R and K. Since S is false, E must hold. Both parts of choice E follow.

Why the others fail: A contradicts the application's completeness. B denies the required remaining award alternative. C contradicts the stated absence of a standard award. D contradicts the completed review established by the grant.
